newsitem.title: UK: OPTIONS - Cable vols at '96 highs, mirror spot.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - Cable vols at '96 highs, mirror spot.

text.p: Cable option volatilities jumped to fresh 1996 highs in European trading on Tuesday, taking their cue from a fiery spot market which saw cable topping $1.65 for the first time since March 1995.
"As cable broke above the $1.65 level it triggered a whole lot of stops and that took the vols even higher, " said an options broker at a UK bank.
One-month cable vols were quoted at 8.90/9.40 percent, their highest level since January, and well above 7.75/8.05 percent on Monday.
The one-month risk-reversal, the difference in implied vols between relative calls and puts, continued to favour sterling calls and traded at 0.8/1.2 percent against 0.6/1.0 on Monday.
"Vols are high but justified given spot's move and tight supply, they are fairly priced," said a U.S. bank options trader.
"Weekly close-to-close historical volatility is roughly around 11.25 percent, while one-week implied is at 10.5 percent. High but still room to move just a bit higher."

Dealers said the cable options market is usually dominated by UK corporate hedgers but many were sidelined by the pound's tight summer ranges around $1.55. But cable's break above $1.60 has seen many hedgers scrambling for cover, soaking up supply and driving vols higher.
One-month sterling/mark vols also gathered steam in Europe, rising to 8.80/9.30 percent against 8.00/8.40 on Tuesday.
The one-month risk-reversal was steady, biased towards sterling calls at 0.5/1.0 percent against 0.6/1.0 on Monday.
Traders said sterling/mark vols were reasonably well bid on the back of the pound's climb to fresh 2-1/2 year highs above 2.50 marks in Europe today.
Traders said sterling volatilities could go higher, but a calmer spot market afer Tuesday's excitement could instigate a retreat in cable volatilities.
"If the (spot) market calms down, then people will start to back off but vols are not likely to retreat too far after the recent moves in spot," said the U.S bank trader.
The dollar spot and options markets were steady to slightly firmer, paying little attention, for instance, to U.S. elections today and Russian President's Boris Yeltsin's heart operation.
"From the options point of view, the thing that excites volatilities is the unexpected," said the trader.
Traders have already discounted the re-election of U.S. President Bill Clinton and maintained Republican control of Congress, though a Democrat "clean sweep" could upset the dollar.
